method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Optometry Australia '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration' (approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022)), 20 claims; LICENCE: No licence or copyright statement in the PDF or on the Optometry Australia site; treated as all rights reserved (read at the PDF itself (no statement found) and https://www.optometry.org.au/). S2: QUOTED from Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0) 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration' (published 14 July 2025), 14 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC12339655). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society-supported clinical guidelines for neovascular AMD (2025, CC BY 4.0, quoted), for the newer agents S1 predates (faricimab, brolucizumab, aflibercept 8 mg), loading and maintenance regimens, switching, PDT, submacular haemorrhage and long-term management. S1 claims and anchors are unchanged. S2's drug table (Table 4, doses and intervals) was stripped with the other tables. Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S2 Table 1 (MNV classification) and Table 3 (AREDS2 supplement doses) added; S2 Tables 2 and 4 (including the drug table) have merged cells and were not extracted. S1 is a PDF with no appended tables.

claims.claim: **AMD is the leading cause of irreversible vision loss in Australians over 50.**
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Smoking is the biggest risk you can change:** it at least doubles AMD risk, so advise every tobacco user to stop.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Five-year progression risk rises steeply with stage:** about 3.1% for early AMD (medium drusen only), but around 47.3% once both eyes have large drusen and pigment change.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Differentials in which neovascularisation forms without drusen:** polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, ocular histoplasmosis, pathological myopia, choroidal rupture, angioid streaks and idiopathic CNV. Consider diabetic macular oedema when the macula shows blood, lipid, exudate or fluid.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Warn about Charles Bonnet syndrome:** people with late AMD and poor sight in both eyes can get visual hallucinations, which are distressing and often need counselling.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **AMD can present before 50:** S2 removed age from its diagnostic criteria for this reason.
claims.source_text: Importantly, AMD are sometimes seen even in patients under 50 years of age, and thus, age was removed from the updated diagnostic criteria.
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Types of macular neovascularisation (S2 Table 1):** type 1 without a polypoidal lesion, type 1 with a polypoidal lesion (PCV), type 2, mixed type 1 and 2, and type 3 (retinal angiomatous proliferation, RAP).
claims.source_text: [Table 1 row 1] Type 1 MNV without polypoidal lesion: Type 1 MNV with polypoidal lesion (PCV) … [Table 1 row 2] Type 1 MNV without polypoidal lesion: Type 2 MNV Mixed type 1 and type 2 MNV … [Table 1 row 3] Type 1 MNV without polypoidal lesion: Type 3 MNV(RAP) … [Table 1 footnote] MNV macular neovascularization, PCV polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, RAP retinal angiomatous proliferation
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV) is a major neovascular AMD subtype in Asian populations;** its first-line treatment has moved to anti-VEGF monotherapy rather than photodynamic therapy alone or in combination.
claims.source_text: In Asian countries, polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV) is considered a major subtype of neovascular AMD, and some cases of PCV develop against a background of pachychoroid []. The first-line treatment for PCV has shifted to monotherapy with anti-VEGF drugs, rather than monotherapy or combination therapy with photodynamic therapy (PDT).
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Suspected or definite new choroidal neovascular membrane: send to an ophthalmologist as an urgent referral, to be seen within one week.** Where ophthalmology is hard to reach, get a telehealth opinion by e-referral in the same week.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Urgent-referral triggers:** vision loss, distortion reported unprompted, or a new missing or blurred patch in central vision within the last 3 months; or signs of new CNV, fluid under or within the retina at the macula, or bleeding there that nothing else explains.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Speed matters:** vision at presentation is among the strongest predictors of long-term acuity, so the sooner treatment starts, the better the chance of keeping or gaining vision.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **OCT is among the most useful tests:** it shows active neovascular disease such as retinal fluid. Get an OCT whenever new symptoms appear or neovascular AMD is suspected, and refer if needed.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection is the mainstay of treatment.** In Australia the main agents are ranibizumab and aflibercept, with bevacizumab used off-label. Their efficacy is similar, so availability, injection frequency and cost usually decide the choice.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Start with injections at fixed monthly intervals until the lesion shows no activity** (for example, no fluid on OCT).
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Treat and extend:** each time there is no sign of active CNV (no OCT fluid, no loss of 5 letters, no new haemorrhage), the gap to the next injection grows by 2 weeks. Visual results match monthly dosing.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **As-needed (PRN), monthly-or-bimonthly and observe-and-plan schedules are options,** but they generally do worse than treat and extend or monthly injections.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Thermal laser and photodynamic therapy are now rare,** kept mostly for polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy with a well-defined lesion away from the fovea.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Current agents (S2, Japan):** ranibizumab (and a biosimilar), aflibercept 2 mg and 8 mg, brolucizumab and faricimab, which targets both VEGF and angiopoietin-2. All improved vision in their pivotal trials, including TENAYA/LUCERNE (faricimab), HAWK/HARRIER (brolucizumab) and PULSAR (aflibercept 8 mg).
claims.source_text: The first-line treatment for neovascular AMD is the intravitreal injection of anti-VEGF drugs []. In Japan, the currently available anti-VEGF drugs for neovascular AMD include ranibizumab (Lucentis® and ranibizumab biosimilar), aflibercept (Eylea® 2 mg and 8 mg), brolucizumab (Beovu®), and faricimab (Vabysmo®), an antibody against VEGF and angiopoietin-2 (Table 4). Representative clinical trials of these drugs (e.g., MARINA study []; ANCHOR study []; VIEW 1/2 study []; HAWK/HARRIER study []; TENAYA/LUCERNE study []; PULSAR study []) demonstrate improved visual acuity.
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Brolucizumab has higher rates of retinal vasculitis and retinal vascular occlusion,** so intraocular inflammation must be found and managed early; inflammation can occur with every anti-VEGF agent.
claims.source_text: Although intraocular inflammation associated with anti-VEGF drugs can occur with all these agents, brolucizumab injection is associated with higher incidences of retinal vasculitis and retinal vascular occlusion, which necessitate early detection and management of intraocular inflammation
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Loading phase: monthly injections, usually three or four in a row depending on the drug,** followed by a maintenance phase to hold the vision gained.
claims.source_text: The loading phase in anti-VEGF therapy refers to the period during which monthly injections (typically administered consecutively three or four times, depending on the drug) are administered to achieve visual acuity improvement. The maintenance phase refers to the subsequent period aimed at stabilizing visual acuity.
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Maintenance: treat-and-extend over as-needed (PRN).** PRN after loading lost vision over two years against monthly injections (CATT, HARBOR), and long-term PRN in practice often let vision slip; treat-and-extend matched fixed dosing and beat PRN, at the cost of more injections. There is no consensus on how long to continue it; fit the plan to the patient's circumstances and the fellow eye.
claims.source_text: However, studies of ranibizumab, such as CATT and HARBOR, demonstrate that PRN treatment following a loading phase resulted in decreased visual acuity over two years compared with monthly injections [, ]. Additionally, long-term PRN treatment in clinical settings has not been effective in maintaining improved visual acuity, instead, deterioration often occurred … Systematic reviews and meta-analyses show that the treat-and-extend regimen provides visual acuity improvements similar to the fixed-dosing regimen over two years []. Additionally, treat-and-extend regimens provide significantly better visual outcomes than PRN regimens, although more frequent injections than the PRN regimen are required []. As yet, there is no consensus on the duration of treat-and-extend regimens. Furthermore, the choice of maintenance-phase dosing should be made flexibly, considering the patient's social circumstances and the condition of the fellow eye.
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Switch anti-VEGF drug** when the response is inadequate or wanes (acquired tolerance), or to ease the treatment burden; for an inadequate response, adding PDT to anti-VEGF is another option.
claims.source_text: If treatment response is inadequate (i.e., resistant cases) or decreases over time (e.g., acquired tolerance), switching to another drug may be effective. Drug switching may be an option considering the treatment burden. … *5: For patients with inadequate or no response to treatment, consider switching anti-VEGF drugs or combining anti-VEGF therapy with PDT.
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **PDT, usually with anti-VEGF, remains an option for PCV** (it improves vision and can fully regress polyps) and for disease resistant to anti-VEGF. Avoid long-term PDT with a thin choroid or existing macular atrophy, and do not use it for type 3 MNV.
claims.source_text: The combination of anti-VEGF drugs and PDT remains one treatment option for PCV and is effective in improving visual acuity and leads to complete polyp regression … PDT may be a potential treatment option for neovascular AMD resistant to anti-VEGF drugs. … Long-term PDT may exacerbate macular atrophy; therefore, it should be avoided in patients with a thin choroid or preexisting macular atrophy. Notably, PDT is currently not recommended for type 3 MNV.
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Massive submacular haemorrhage causes sudden, irreversible loss.** Caught early, it can be displaced with intravitreal gas or vitrectomy, sometimes with anti-VEGF or off-label tPA, to improve vision.
claims.source_text: Neovascular AMD can cause massive submacular hemorrhage, leading to a sudden and significant decline in visual acuity (Fig. 5). Damage to the outer retina due to submacular hemorrhage causes irreversible vision loss. If detected early, visual improvements can be achieved by displacing the submacular hemorrhage (Fig. 15). Submacular hemorrhage displacement may be performed using intravitreal gas injection or vitrectomy [, ]. During these procedures, intravitreal injections of anti-VEGF drugs or tissue plasminogen activator (tPA, off-label use) may be used in combination.
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Neovascular AMD cannot be cured and needs long-term management:** activity recurs, and the fellow eye often develops MNV. Eyes with scarring, very poor vision and little activity are better observed than treated further.
claims.source_text: Even when the activity of MNV temporarily subsides, it may recur over a long period, and repeated exudation can result in atrophic changes or fibrotic scarring leading to significant vision loss. Moreover, MNV frequently develops in the fellow eye, therefore, long-term management is necessary to avoid irreversible vision loss bilaterally. … For patients with significantly reduced visual acuity, with low disease activity, further treatments are less helpful. Instead, such patients should be considered for observational management.
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Judge activity on OCT by exudation** (intraretinal, subretinal or sub-RPE fluid, haemorrhage, fibrin) and scan the whole macula or lesion: the most active part (polyps in PCV, intraretinal vessels in type 3 MNV) may lie away from the fovea.
claims.source_text: Disease activity in neovascular AMD refers to exudative changes (e.g., fluid, fibrin, hemorrhage, etc.) arising from MNV. Activity can be assessed using OCT, which non-invasively detects fluid accumulation around the MNV and differentiates IRF, SRF, and sub-RPE fluids. … Importantly, the entire macula or lesion should be scanned to accurately assess fluid and SHRM, as the site of high disease activity in MNV, particularly polypoidal lesions in PCV or intraretinal neovascularization in type 3 MNV, does not necessarily involve the fovea.
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **The guide notes no approved treatment for geographic atrophy;** review it every six to twelve months, with the interval set by vision, driving status and risk of progression, and offer low-vision care. It can convert to neovascular AMD, so teach Amsler-grid use.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **For intermediate AMD, the AREDS2 formula may help:** vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 IU, zinc 80 mg (as zinc oxide), copper 2 mg (as cupric oxide), lutein 10 mg and zeaxanthin 2 mg. ⚠️ That zinc dose is above the Australian and New Zealand upper intake limit, so discuss it with the GP.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **S2 describes AREDS2 differently:** lutein/zeaxanthin in place of beta-carotene (which raises lung-cancer risk in smokers) and zinc cut from 80 mg to 25 mg, with no loss of benefit. Supplements do not stop early AMD becoming intermediate, and excess vitamins and zinc can cause harm.
claims.source_text: As beta-carotene intake in smokers is associated with an increased risk of lung cancer, AREDS2 recommends replacing beta-carotene with lutein/zeaxanthin and reducing zinc intake from 80 mg to 25 mg. Moreover, AREDS2 demonstrates no difference in preventive efficacy following these alterations (Table 3) [, ]. Current evidence does not support the hypothesis that supplements can prevent the progression from early to intermediate AMD. Furthermore, the excessive intake of vitamins and zinc may have side effects; therefore, caution is necessary when using these supplements.
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **S2's AREDS2 table (daily doses):** vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 IU, lutein/zeaxanthin 10 mg/2 mg, zinc (as zinc oxide) 25 mg and copper (as cupric oxide) 2 mg.
claims.source_text: [Table 3 row 1] Components: Vitamin C Vitamin E Lutein/zeaxanthin Zinc oxide Cupric oxide · Daily intake: 500 mg 400 IU 10 mg/2 mg 25 mg 2 mg
claims.locator: Iida T, Gomi F, Yasukawa T, Yamashiro K, et al. (working group supported by the Japanese Retina and Vitreous Society), Japanese Journal of Ophthalmology 69:639 (doi 10.1007/s10384-025-01240-0), 'Japanese clinical guidelines for neovascular age-related macular degeneration', published 14 July 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12339655/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Supplements are not advised** for early AMD, for normal age-related changes only, when both eyes already have late AMD, or for at-risk people without any AMD signs.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Teach home Amsler-grid monitoring at every visit,** and tell the patient to come in at once for distortion, central blur or vision loss.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Review without new symptoms:** early AMD at least every 12 months; intermediate AMD every 6 to 12 months (per the guide's review table).
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Early or intermediate AMD does not need an ophthalmologist** unless there is a strong family history (possible inherited dystrophy), atypical findings including onset before age 50, or the patient wants to join a trial.
claims.locator: Optometry Australia, '2019 Clinical Practice Guide for the diagnosis, treatment and management of age-related macular degeneration', approved 8 February 2019 (due for revision 2022), https://www.optometry.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Professional_support/Practice_notes/AMD-Clinical-Practice-Guide-2019_final_designed_v5.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23
